newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel says Genzyme's Carticel effective.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel says Genzyme's Carticel effective.

text.p: A Food and Drug Administration advisory panel said Thursday that Genzyme Corp's Carticel treatment for knee cartilage repair seems to help patients but called for more long-term study on why the procedure works.

The panel was faced with an unusual situation because the product is already on the market and available to surgeons and their patients. It involves an innovative method of harvesting the patient's cartilage cells, culturing them and then using them in surgery to correct the injury.
The FDA has only recently begun to regulate such cell and tissue products, known as biologics.
The FDA panel did not vote on whether the FDA should formally approve Carticel but their finding that it is safe and effective paves the way for FDA approval.

The Cambridge, Mass.-based company, one of the U.S. leaders in biotechnology, has touted its cell treatment as a groundbreaking therapy. But the FDA panelists said there was not yet enough research to establish with certainty that it was the treated cells that were responsisble for the patients' improvement, rather than the overall surgery and rehabilitation program.

About 70 percent of the patients who have undergone the treatment improved, which the panelists said seems to be a better rate than conventional treatment. Repairing knee cartilage has been one of the great unsolved problems of orthopedics.

Genzyme estimates that up to 200,000 to 300,000 patients in the United States and Europe could be candidates for the treatment each year. The company has estimated that each treatment could generate sales of $10,000.

However, analysts say that the market will depend on how much acceptance Carticel gets from surgeons. David Stone, an analyst at Cowen Inc in Boston, said most of the surgeons who have received training in the technique have not yet used it.
"Some are very enthusiastic -- a small group of surgeons have done most of the treatments. But others think this is not ready for prime time yet," Stone said.
